Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

items.title: Is Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The Latest
items.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with John Collingridge; produced by Angus Neale; senior producer Leonore Schick; executive producer Zoe Hitch
items.content:
The AI firm and Claude chatbot maker Anthropic has made a historic stock market debut, with a peak valuation of $1.3tn on its first day of trading. It marks a remarkable ascent for a start-up launched in just 2021 by a group of ex-OpenAI staffers. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said the record-breaking IPO had ‘strengthened’ the company’s resolve to ‘do the right thing’. Despite the excitement, the Guardian’s head of business John Collingridge tells Lucy Hough that there are still challenges ahead for the global AI industry

The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme

After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed?

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.content:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?

items.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
items.author: Kevin Rawlinson and Aisha Down
items.content:
News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks

A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.

items.title: ‘Gloucestershire nouveau’: UK vineyard uncorks its 2026 answer to beaujolais
items.author: Joanna Partridge
items.content:
Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years

Forget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest.

Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine.

items.title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park
items.author: Matthew Weaver
items.content:
Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands

The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset.

Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory.

items.title: These US fishers see offshore wind as a ‘godsend’. Trump wants to shut it down
items.author: Hilary Beaumont with photographs by Simon Simard
items.content:
Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream

On a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island.

“God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy.

Continue reading...

items.title: An entrepreneur fights for workers’ protections after his mom was fired after being assaulted at her Saks Fifth Avenue job
items.author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
items.content:
Jeff Vinokur is using his newly minted wealth from the sale of his edtech company to hold the retail store accountable

Late in the afternoon of 28 June, Jeff Vinokur received a call from his mother that sent him running. “I was assaulted,” Vinokur, a popular science educator known as the “Dancing Scientist”, recalled his mother saying.

Vinokur’s mother, Laza Susuni, was working in the women’s ready-to-wear section at Manhattan’s Saks Fifth Avenue that day when a client attacked her in the dressing room. A court document reviewed by the Guardian corroborates that a woman was arrested at that location on assault and harassment charges.

Continue reading...

items.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
items.author: Mark Sweney
items.content:
Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Continue reading...

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.author: Henrietta Moore
items.content:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.title: How to get a bigger Black Friday bargain: cashback, price matches and gift cards
items.author: Hilary Osborne
items.content:
From cashback on what you buy to cut-price gift cards, we offer tips on how to maximise savings on your shopping

With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to entice us to open our wallets.

It could be a great time to snap up the things on your Christmas list or buy household items you need yourself. And there are ways to maximise your savings on Black Friday – which this year falls on 27 November – by doubling up on discounts, or earning cashback on your purchases.

items.title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
items.author: Garrison Lovely
items.content:
Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm

You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.

Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase. On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down. In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.

items.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
items.author: Sarah Marsh
items.content:
Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019

The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning.

Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays.

items.title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
items.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
items.content:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.

items.title: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
items.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
items.content:
A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges

In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading.

With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months.

items.title: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
items.author: Dan Milmo and Aisha Down
items.content:
The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price.

items.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
items.author: Nils Pratley
items.content:
Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask

Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company.

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees.

items.author: Lauren Almeida
items.content:
Citizens Advice criticises company for failing to meet Ofcom requirements while reporting increased revenue

Royal Mail has been accused of offering a “pot luck service” to consumers as it looks likely to miss first-class delivery targets for the fourth consecutive year.

items.title: Nvidia approaches Arm boss Rene Haas in search for new CEO
items.author: Lauren Almeida
items.content:
CEO of Cambridge-based firm viewed as leading contender to replace co-founder Jensen Huang according to reports

Nvidia’s headhunters have reportedly approached the chief executive of the Cambridge-based chip company Arm, in its search for a new leader after Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit.

Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company’s board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg.

items.title: Outages, spies, and trillion-dollar IPOs: is this our AI future? – Stateside with Kai and Carter
items.author: Hosted by Kai Wright , produced by Suzanne Gaber and Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Rachel Humphreys
items.content:
It has been a wild few weeks in the world of tech. First, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, forced an unimaginable leadership change at Nvidia – arguably the most consequential company in AI development. Then, chaos erupted as a rolling set of IT outages disrupted flights, banking, tech companies and the federal government. And now, Anthropic is blowing minds with a trillion-dollar IPO – one of the largest in stock market history. The Atlantic’s tech writer Charlie Warzel tells Kai Wright that these events are linked: they’re all examples of the ways in which we shoulder unprecedented risk today, in order to bet on AI’s future reward. It’s a convoluted logic that keeps the AI race speeding forward, no matter how many warning signs it blows past. Charlie Warzel is also host of the Atlantic’s podcast Galaxy Brain.

Continue reading...

items.title: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover
items.author: Jillian Ambrose
items.content:
Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier

EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita.

Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed.

items.title: BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business
items.author: Lauren Almeida and Jasper Jolly
items.content:
Cuts – which exclude shop floor and aircraft maintenance – prompt calls for more orders to support British defence contractor

The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.

items.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
items.author: Lucy Mangan
items.content:
Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his conviction.

Continue reading...

items.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
items.author: Phillip Inman
items.content:
UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash

Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.

Continue reading...

items.title: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds
items.author: Joanna Partridge
items.content:
About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users

At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined.

About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator.

items.title: Private renters in England: have you struggled to get your deposit back?
items.author: Guardian community team
items.content:
We would like to hear from private tenants about their experiences of the rental deposit system in England

In May 2026, the government overhauled private renting by abolishing no-fault evictions and shifting private tenancies to rolling contracts. However, deposit protection remains an issue for many private renters.

The government has promised and begun consulting on reforms, including scrapping insured deposit schemes, but has yet to confirm when this will happen. Landlords and letting agents are currently permitted to hold tenant deposits in their own bank accounts and this creates a “power imbalance”, housing and planning minister Matthew Pennycook has said.

Continue reading...

items.title: UK energy bills are rising. Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal?
items.author: Guardian community team
items.content:
We’d like to hear from UK households about whether they’re switching energy suppliers to save money or finding that deals are too similar to make it worthwhile

Energy bills in Great Britain are forecast to rise by 26% from January, adding £443 to the typical household’s annual bill. The increase, driven by rising gas prices amid the Middle East conflict, would be one of the biggest quarterly rises on record, according to forecaster Cornwall Insight.

Are you shopping around for a better gas or electricity deal or have you decided to stay with your current supplier? What has influenced your decision?

Continue reading...

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.author: Hilary Osborne Consumer and money editor
items.content:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

Continue reading...

items.title: Smoke spews from landfill in California after gas release – video
items.content:
A release of gas at the Chiquita Canyon landfill in Castaic, California, sent smoke billowing into the air and prompted an evacuation, the Los Angeles county fire department said. The department said workers doing routine digging in an area that had not been worked on for some time hit a deposit of gases. Officials initially said a pipe had been struck. There was no fire, only smoke, and a hazardous materials team was sent in with air monitoring in place, according to local media

items.title: Can Labour end the youth unemployment crisis? – podcast
items.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal; produced by George McDonagh, Ivor Manley , Harriet Mogie and Rudi Zygadlo; executive producer Eli Block
items.content:
There are about a million young people across the country not in employment, education or training. Could Alan Milburn’s landmark report help change that? reports

The UK has one of the worst rates in Europe when it comes to youth unemployment. From the savage cuts to youth services during austerity, to the impacts of the pandemic and now the threat of AI to entry level jobs, young people across the country are feeling that the social contract is broken.

But now Alan Milburn, the 68-year-old New Labour veteran, has published a radical review urging the government to spend billions on a new deal for young people.

Continue reading...

items.title: A potato war has been simmering for decades between the US and Japan. It’s about to reach boiling point
items.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
items.content:
Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which farmers say would threaten their livelihoods

It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato.

Along with rice, the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food.

Continue reading...

items.title: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
items.author: Jessica Murray  and Neha Gohil
items.content:
Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial

When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country.

The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence.

Continue reading...

items.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
items.author: Donna Ferguson. Photographs by Urszula Sołtys for the Guardian
items.content:
Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm
